replying_to: Replying to Active Learning: Sampling in the Least Probable Disagreement Region
display_title: Official Review of Paper1379 by Reviewer VT7X

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose an active learning (AL) strategy where they adaptively select the most informative unlabeled instances on their distance to the decision boundary, and query them to improve the training of a classifier. In order to quantify this distance, they introduce a measure, the so-called least probable disagreement region (LPDR). Further, they introduce a hypothesis sampling method, which extracts the order of LPDR measures of samples without explicitly computing them, and query the labels of instances that are in the LPDR. The effectiveness of the method is illustrated on a large set of experiments. The proposed AL strategy seems to outperform the state-of-the-art methods on a variety of datasets.
content.main_review:
*Strengths:* The idea of perturbing the decision boundary to find out the most uncertain data instances seems promising and intuitive in AL. The assumptions made in the paper are put in conjecture form, and empirically justified in Appendix. The experiments seem extensive and the numerical results seem promising -- especially given how hard it is to compete with the existing AL strategies. 

*Weaknesses:* The main result in Theorem 2 is a bit limiting as it concerns only the linear classifiers in the binary classification setting. I am not so clear on why this disagree ratio would be the best. _Did the authors investigate further measures such as entropy? (while sampling the classifiers the same way -- which is not the same as the classical entropy-based sampling)_ 
I also sought for some other experimental details in the main body such as some implementation details on the existing methods, or initial label size, etc. I found them mostly in Appendix.

*Further questions:*
* Could the authors clarify how did they tune $\beta$ at the update step of $\sigma$ in the DRAL algorithm? How sensitive is the method to this hyperparameter?
* Is table 2 in %?
* How was the entropy method implemented? As in, how were the classifiers formed such that the entropy of an instance can be measured?
* As the query size is always at least the initial label size, how do the authors predict the behavior of their method when the initial label size is much smaller than what is used in the results? It would be helpful to see the results in a larger practical regime, i.e., the initial label size is 1-10% of the entire unlabeled pool, etc. This might be good to know as the method heavily relies on the labeled data so far, hence the wrong selection made at the beginning of the process might propagate.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea of perturbing the decision boundary to measure the uncertainty of an instance in AL is promising, and the effectiveness of this idea is sufficiently demonstrated on a set of experiments. In my opinion, this paper is marginally above the acceptance threshold.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer VT7X
content.comment:
$\bullet$ The main result in Theorem 2 is --

: Theorem 2 concerns binary classification with linear classifier for it is hard to prove in multiclass classification with deep networks. The empirical result for multiclass classification with the deep network can be seen in Figure 2a--the disagree ratios of all samples go to 0 as $\sigma \rightarrow 0$ and goes to $1-1/n_c$ as $\sigma \rightarrow \infty$ where $n_c$ is the number of class. The disagree ratio is not chosen among various measures but is induced from the definition of LPDR, a measure of the sample's sensitiveness to perturbation of the decision boundary. The experimental details for existing methods initially labeled size, and hyperparameters are moved from Appendix to main body.


$\bullet$ Could the authors clarify how did they tune $\beta$ --

: We investigate the effect of hyperparameters $\beta$, $N$, and the sampling layer, and the results for $\beta \in \\{0.1, 1, 10\\}$ show that there is no significant performance difference with respect to $\beta$. Thus, we set $\beta = 1$ for convenience. The details of results for hyperparameters is in Appendix I.	


$\bullet$ Is table 2 in \%? 

: Yes, we added (\%) in the paper.	


$\bullet$ How was the entropy method implemented? --

: In the paper, entropy is obtained as follows:
\begin{equation*}
	\mathbb{H} [y|\boldsymbol{x}, \mathcal{L}] = - \sum_c \mathbb{P}[y=c|\boldsymbol{x}, \mathcal{L}] \log (\mathbb{P}[y=c|\boldsymbol{x}, \mathcal{L}]).
\end{equation*}
For the prediction of $\mathbb{P}[y=c|\boldsymbol{x}, \mathcal{L}]$, we use the single trained classifier.	




$\bullet$ As the query size is always at least the initial label size, --

: The additional experiments for the effects of initial labeled size on the proposed algorithm are conducted on MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets, and there is no significant performance difference with respect to the initial labeled size. The details of the results are added to Appendix L.

$\bullet$ Reply to summary -- 

: Thank you for your positive evaluation of this paper.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1379 by Reviewer nHiD

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a new active learning technique based on the Least probable disagreement region. Basically, it proposes to measure how interesting it would be to learn a label of an instance x by measuring the lowest probability of disagreement  that a disagreeing model with $\hat{h}$ (the currently optimal model) on x would have. The lower is this probability, the more desirable it is to elicit the label of x, as it is likely to sit on the decision border.

The rest of the paper is dedicated to how approximate this value computationally, as it is in practice hard to estimate. The resulting approximation is then tested on a bunch of data sets and deep learning models.
content.main_review:
While I think the paper idea is interesting to investigate, the paper makes many assumptions, some unproved or whose plausibility was hard for me to assess, that makes the theoretical aspects of the proposal hard to really assess. In particular:

* Most of the theoretical analysis and results rely on the satisfaction of Proposition 1, that requires the set of hypothesis to be large enough so that it satisfies an inequality (involving the non-estimable $L_{\hat{h}}(x)$).

* While the graph in appendix C1 are mostly increasing, this is not exactly true for all of them, for instance HAM10000 around 0 value for $\log(\sigma)$. As one counter-example is enough to disprove a conjecture, this puts a serious question mark around the presented conjecture. Most of the curves also do not appear to be entirely continuous. Do the authors really think that this is true, and if so what prevented them from proving them? 

* Conjecture 2 is even more dubious, as many graphs did not even reach the value -1, which would have been needed to have a positive example that indeed such a perfect $\sigma_*$ could exist? It is very hard to conclude from those graphs that the conjecture would indeed be true. And something that is "mostly true" should not appear as a conjecture, which is usually used to replace a theorem/proposition authors think is true but could not prove? 

Some part of the paper are also really dense, making the paper sometimes hard to follow, for instance:

* The whole paragraph after Conjecture 1 is quite hard to follow, and I must admit I missed some intuition here to fully understand it. Also, the index $(k)$ suddenly appears out of the blue (I gather this means that we are at the $k$th query)? 

Also, the end-resulting approximation and techniques seems to me quite standard, as it amounts to be counting, within an ensemble of models, the number of models disagreeing with the current one. Form this follows two comments:

* one may wonder why the paper focus solely on comparing with deep active learning techniques, whereas it should also show that it has good results with generic learners and recent active learning techniques not dedicated to deep learning techniques. For instance, one could look at (Nguyen, Vu-Linh, Mohammad Hossein Shaker, and Eyke Hüllermeier. "How to measure uncertainty in uncertainty sampling for active learning." Machine Learning (2021): 1-34.)

* It should also discuss the differences with those standard active learning techniques, and why this new one should be better and/or equivalent? Clearly, reducing the discussion to deep learning is a bit frustrating in this case (although probably fashionable). 

As a final comments, I would also say that while the results seem to be promising for the considered method (but I must say I am not familiar with the other baselines, except entropy which is questionable with uncalibrated probability estimates), I am a bit dubious about having strong experts tagging thousands of examples correctly (as the framework assume that labels are given without mistakes).
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper explores what could be an interesting idea, but I miss a larger discussion comparing and discussing the merits of the approach with standard or recent active learning approaches not especially focusing on deep approaches. Also, it is quite hard at times to see if the theoretical part of the paper is firmly grounded, as the support and plausibility of conjectures and hypothesis is kind of hard to assess, if not questionable to some extent.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer nHiD
content.comment:
$\bullet$ Most of the theoretical analysis and results --

: As you mentioned, for empirical LPDR to converge to LPDR, the size of $\mathcal{H}\_C$, i.e., $C$, should go to $\infty$. With relatively small $C$, it cannot be known how well the empirical LPDR approximates the LPDR for the LPDR cannot be evaluated explicitly in practice. However, in the experimental results, it has been confirmed that algorithm with disagree ratio of sampled hypotheses performs well.	


$\bullet$ While the graph in appendix C1 are mostly increasing, --

: A part of Conjecture 1 has been revised and the theoretical verification for binary classification with linear classifier is provided in Appendix C. The empirical verification in the paper is conducted with relatively small finite set of sampled hypotheses, thus the empirical results may not exactly true for all of them. Although it cannot be proven or explicitly verified in deep networks, we believe that the conjecture will be satisfied as the number of sampled hypotheses goes to infinity.   


$\bullet$ Conjecture 2 is even more dubious, --

: A part of Conjecture 2 has been revised and the theoretical verification for binary classification with linear classifier is provided in Appendix C. As with the empirical verification for Conjecture 1, the empirical verification for Conjecture 2 is conducted with relatively small finite set of sampled hypotheses. It still cannot be proven or explicitly verified in deep networks, we believe that the conjecture will be satisfied as the number of sampled hypotheses goes to infinity. 	


$\bullet$ The whole paragraph after Conjecture 1 is quite hard to follow, --

: The paragraph describes the process of constructing $\mathcal{H}\_C$ for evaluating empirical LPDR of a sample to the learned hypothesis, and it has been revised for clarity. The $\mathcal{H}\_C$ is constructed by the union of sampled hypothesis sets with gradually increasing $\sigma$.


$\bullet$ Also, the end-resulting approximation and techniques seems to me quite standard, --

: First, the proposed algorithm (DRAL and DRAL$^+$) seems to be similar with ensemble method from a technical point of view, however it is fundamentally different. The ensemble method does not consider the sample's closeness to the decision boundary since it is based on the voting of the committee as experts by forming a committee with independently trained models. However, the proposed algorithm does not consider $\mathcal{H}\_C$ as a committee composed of independent experts, but finds samples sensitive to perturbation of the decision boundary by investigating the vicinity of the decision boundary using the Monte-Carlo method, which is attributed to the newly defined LPDR in this paper. If the label of a sample can be altered even with a small change in the model, this sample can be considered to be uncertain for this model, and it is understood that the proposed algorithm performs well for it is based on the measure of this sensitivity of the sample to the perturbation of the decision boundary.
Second, thank you for recommending a good paper on uncertainty sampling for active learning, and this paper has been cited in the paper. This paper begins with the question of why uncertainty-based strategies do not consider the plausible assumption that 'the sample closest to the decision boundary is most uncertain and therefore the most informative' in active learning with deep networks. And as an answer to this question, this paper defines an evaluable 'closeness measure' in deep networks and proposes a method to use it for active learning with deep networks. Thus, this paper focuses on deep network and compares with deep active learning techniques.	


$\bullet$ As a final comments, 

: We consider the standard active learning scenario, which assumes that oracle provides true labels. In this scenario, the role of an algorithm is to select samples for which to query the oracle for their labels, and labeling the selected samples is a framework outside the algorithm.


$\bullet$ Reply to summary --

: The proof for Theorem 1 has been revised more firmly and theoretical verifications for Conjecture 1 & 2 are added in Appendix, and it helps to assess the support and plausibility of conjectures or hypothesis.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1379 by Reviewer Urni

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a new sampling strategy for active learning (DRAL) that
stems from a new measure of informativeness of samples: LPDR. In short, LPDR of
a data point $x$ for a hypothesis $h$ is the smallest disagreement probability
of hypotheses that disagree on $x$. It is argued that this measure is related to
closeness to decision boundary, hence the data point with smallest LPDRs are
those considered most informative.


The intuition conveyed in the paper is that if one "perturbs" the decision
boundary a little (by selecting a hypothesis that has small disagreement
probability from $h$), if the label of $x$ changes, this means that $x$ has low
LPDR for $h$, hence close to the decision boundary. 

All the relevant quantities for evaluating the LPDR cannot be computed exactly
in general, and empirical estimates for these quantities are provided in the
paper. For estimating the disagreement probability, a standard sample average is
used, while for estimating LPDR, one has to construct a finite class of
hypotheses in such a way to get a good estimate. In the paper, one way of
estimating is conjectured (empirical LPDR).

It is further conjectured that for specific perturbations of hypotheses,
empirical LPDR is equivalent to disagreement ratio (the ratio of hypotheses that
disagree on $x$ with $h$ among a sampled set of hypotheses). Hence, one can
simply run the disagreement ratio active learning instead of empirical LPDR. 

The paper provides experiments on real datasets and provides a comparison with
STOA. The authors provide empirical insights on their choices and all relevant
plots are present in the paper.
content.main_review:
All in all, the paper touches upon an important question. 
It provides a good list of prior works with their weaknesses. The authors
provide a compilation of plots in accordance to their assumptions throughout. 

The experimental results are quite promising, with the proposed method
outperforming many existing methods for active learning on neural networks. The
authors perform several sets of experiments which give good insight into the
general power and robustness of the methods.

However, I am concerned about a few points which I list below:
- The discussion about why LPDR is corresponding to the closeness to the
  decision boundary is not very thorough. As one of the main contributions of
  the paper, I expected to see more relations between these two quantities. Only
  for the case of linear classifier with fixed weights, it is described and it
  is not clear whether there is a general relation between these two (the
  intuition I wrote above might be a good hand-wavy start, but a rigorous
  treatment is missing) 

- In the proof of __Theorem 1__, I cannot follow the conclusions made by (4) and (5). Here is my understanding: 
Fix $\hat{h}, x, \epsilon > 0$. Take $C$ large enough that Property 1 holds. By Hoeffding and a union bound, on an event $A$ with probability at least $1 - 2C\exp(-2\epsilon^2 S)$ one has a good uniform approximation of $\rho(h_c, \hat{h})$ through its empirical estimate $\rho_S(h_c, \hat{h})$: 

   $$
    \forall h_c \in \mathcal{H}_C(\hat{h}, c), \quad |\rho_S(h_c, \hat{h}) -
    \rho(h_c, \hat{h})| < \epsilon.
  $$

  The next step is to take an arbitrary $h \in \mathcal{H}(\hat{h}, x)$. Then, by Property 1, there __exists__ some $h_c = h_c(h) \in \mathcal{H}_C(\hat{h}, x)$ such that

  $$
    |\rho(h_c, \hat{h}) - \rho(h, \hat{h})| \leq \epsilon.
  $$

  I stress again that $h_c$ depends on $h$. Combining these two inequalities gives the following on event $A$:

  $$
    \rho(h, \hat{h}) \leq \rho(h_c(h), \hat{h}) + \epsilon \leq \rho_S(h_c(h), \hat{h}) + 2\epsilon,
  $$

  and similarly, a lower bound. The authors proceed by taking an infimum over all $h\in\mathcal{H}(\hat{h}, x)$ from both sides. The left hand side becomes $L_{\hat{h}}(x)$ by definition, while the authors claim that the right hand side becomes 
$\inf_{h_c \in \mathcal{H}_C(\hat{h}, x)}{\rho_S(h_c, \hat{h})}+2\epsilon$.

 However, note that in the inequality above, $h_c$ _depends_ on $h$, hence, the infimum $\inf_{h\in \mathcal{H}(\hat{h}, x)} \rho_S(h_c(h), \hat{h}) + 2\epsilon$ is in general _bigger_ than the infimum over all possible $h_c$. I might be confused, and would be delighted if the authors elaborate on this matter. 

- In the same proof, there is an asymmetry between $\epsilon$ and $C$. Property 1 states that for every $C$ there is an $\epsilon_C$ and if $C \to \infty$, then $\epsilon_C \to 0$. Hence, in the consistency proof (given that the computations before are correct), we get that with probability at least

  $$
    1 - 2Ce^{-2\epsilon_C^2 S},
  $$

  empirical LPDR is $\epsilon_C$-close to LPDR. Then it is claimed that as $\min(S, C) \to \infty$ and $(\log C)/S \to 0$ this probability converges to 1. A problem of this argument is that $\epsilon_C$ is not fixed; as an example consider $\epsilon_C = \frac{1}{C}$ and set $S = C = n$. All the conditions are satisfied by this example, while the limit of $1 - 2ne^{-2/n}$ as $n \to \infty$ is $-\infty$! This means that $S$ must be _much_ larger than $1/\epsilon_C^2$ for the bounds to be nonvacuous. I believe the rate of decrease of $\epsilon_C$ is crucial, even for proving asymptotic consistency with the techniques used by the authors (union bound and Hoeffding).

- In the proof of rank-order consistency, I do not understand how the LDPRs of $x_i$ are distinct. Also I quite did not understand how uniform convergence is implied by (5).

- Statement of the Conjecture 1 is not clear for me. What does it mean to be
  increasing in the limit? in which sense?

- In the fourth line after Conjecture 1, how the argument about the diameter is concluded? ($\max_{\cdots} \min_{\cdots} |\rho_S(\cdots) - \rho_S(\cdots)| \leq \epsilon_C$). The assumptions made on the previous line are about expectation.

- In the third line before section 4.2, why the assumption about existence of such $\sigma_*$ is plausible? This assumption seems to be very strong (and I believe is one of the important points of the paper that DR is a good proxy for empirical LPDR) and looks like assuming the solution. I would appreciate it a lot if the authors provide a more rigorous ground on this assumption.

- The conjectures made in the paper (Conjectures 1 and 2) are hard for me to relate to. It would be nice if the authors made the conjectures a bit more general and concluded some parts of their work given the conjectures. At the end of the day, a good conjecture is something that ignites research on a problem.

### minor comments
- Figure 1a might be misleading. The data distribution is of course important
  for the LPDR, and some specific data distribution should be chosen/described for the figure.

- flow: last two lines before 3.2 is detached. 
- second line of section 3.1: $h:\mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$. 
- next line: disagreement metric is defined as the probability of the
  disagreement region ...
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe that this paper is a good start, but not grounded, neither mathematically nor intuitively. The flow of the paper suggests that LPDR is going to be the method to be implemented, but suddenly, with an extra inline assumption, the whole paper suddenly shifts towards sampling a batch of hypothesis from a normal distribution over the weights and look at their disagreement ratio. While the experiments are showing that such a method might actually work, I still believe that more thoughts and rigorous arguments are needed to put this paper in the context of other active learning papers. Specifically, a simple study case (e.g., linear classifiers) with rigorous sample complexity bounds and theoretical verification of the assumptions made in the paper would shed a lot of light on this method.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer Urni
content.comment:
$\bullet$ The discussion about why LPDR is corresponding to the closeness -- 

: The closeness considered in the paper is not a spatial measure in instance space such as Euclidean distance between a sample and the decision boundary. We consider the closeness as the sensitiveness to the small perturbation of the decision boundary, and the LPDR is a measure of this closeness in terms of the disagree metric between the learned hypothesis and a hypothesis that can alter the predicted label of the sample. LPDR is consistent with Euclidean distance in the binary classification with linear classifier with fixed weights in the previous manuscript, but it is not consistent with Euclidean distance in Figure 1a of the revised paper. Therefore, LPDR and closeness are not related as individual indicators, but LPDR is a newly defined closeness indicator.

$\bullet$ In the proof of Theorem 1, --

: Please see the revised manuscript for the comprehensive understanding related to the infimum.  To improve readability, we modified and added details in the proof. The key point of the corrected proof in the infimum convergence is that $\mathcal{H}\_C \subset \mathcal{H}$ and $ \inf_{h_c \in \mathcal{H}\_C} \rho_{S} ( h_c, \hat{h} ) \to \inf_{h_c \in \mathcal{H}\_C} \rho ( h_c, \hat{h} ),$ which is used to prove the upper bound of the infimum convergence. We clarify this in the revised manuscript.        

$\bullet$ In the same proof, --

: By careful observations, we ensure that the proof of Theorem 1 is sufficient with any $\epsilon>0.$ We drop the index $C$ in $\epsilon_{_C}$ in Property 1 in the revised manuscripts to avoid any confusion. Also, the proof of Theorem 1 is refined and supplemented with detailed explanations.

Note that in Theorem 1, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $  \inf_{i \neq j} | L_{\hat{h}} ( \boldsymbol{x}\_i ) -  L_{\hat{h}} ( \boldsymbol{ x}\_j ) |  > \delta$, which makes the proof of Theorem 1  sufficient with any $\epsilon>0.$    


$\bullet$ In the proof of rank-order consistency, --

: We assume that LPDRs of $ \boldsymbol{x}_i$ are distinct since the same $\boldsymbol{x}_i$s conclude the same LPDRs, which is not meaningful in the rank of LPDR. Therefore, we consider the distinct LPDRs on finite $\boldsymbol{x}_i$s. The uniform convergence implied by (5) is explained in a detailed manner in the proof of Theorem 1 of the revised manuscript.  


$\bullet$ Statement of the Conjecture 1 is not clear for me. --

: It means that $\mathbb{E} [\rho(h, \hat{h})]$ is increasing with $\sigma$, and $\mathbb{E} [\rho_{_S} (h, \hat{h})] \rightarrow \mathbb{E} [\rho(h, \hat{h})]$ as $S \rightarrow \infty$. For clarity, the statement of Conjecture 1 is revised.	


$\bullet$ In the fourth line after Conjecture 1, --

: The statement is somewhat ambiguous and has been corrected. 


$\bullet$ In the third line before section 4.2, --

: As you mentioned, the assumption about the existence of $\sigma_*$ is very strong, thus we revised the statement. The point is that samples with small LPDR are more sensitive to perturbation of the decision boundary, thus the labels of the samples are more likely to be altered by the hypothesis perturbation. The inverse relation between LPDR and DR is inferred by the process: LPDR is small $\rightarrow$ more sensitive $\rightarrow$ label is altered more often $\rightarrow$ more disagreement with learned hypothesis $\rightarrow$ DR is large.  


$\bullet$ The conjectures made in the paper (Conjectures 1 and 2) are hard for me to relate to. --

: The statements of Conjecture 1 and 2 are revised, and theoretical verification for binary classification with linear classifier is added to Appendix C.

$\bullet$ Reply to summary --

: First, the statement for `extra inline assumption' is revised to smooth the flow of the paper. This paper defines LPDR as a measure of closeness and introduces a practical method for determining the sample order in terms of LPDR. Therefore, hypothesis sampling and disagree ratio are not introduced suddenly and should be understood as a practical algorithm of LPDR-based active learning. Next, the theoretical verification of conjectures for the binary classification with the linear classifier is provided in Appendix C.  


$\bullet$ Minor issues --

: We revised the paper following your comments.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper builds up in the idea of the classical most uncertain query strategy, where  the closeness of a sample to decision boundary is used / needed. However, the paper claims that when using DNNs in multi-class classification, it is harder to identify samples close to the decision boundary as the sample’s closeness based on Euclidean distance is often not readily measurable.

The paper proposes the idea of the LPDR region: a closeness measure that can be evaluated in multi-class classification with deep network as a measure of uncertainty. They assume that the most uncertain and thus the most informative samples will have their labels most “sensitive” to the smallest perturbation of the decision boundary.
content.main_review:
Pros:

- The paper is well written and it is easy to understand and follow. I has appropriate references.
- Experiments seem sufficient and they are well documented in the appendix.
- There seems to be marginal improvements wrt other existing methods

Weaknesses: 
 - when to sampling w for  large models with millions of parameters, I am skeptical about the quality of the estimation of the disagreement D. I guess N has to be bigger. how big it was in the experiments, I don't think I saw that in the paper. it seems like it could be more robust  for linear models with an smaller number of parameters.
- Is the whole parameter set resampled in the experiments or only the last layer?, I guess the answer seems to be yes but did you considered resampling only a few of the last layers?
 - A concern is that the results are fine but marginal in MNIST, CIFAR10 and SVHN
	Adding the number of parameters to be samples by model would be useful information for the experimental results. For example: how many parameter have WRN-16-8,  is it ~11MM parameters?
	The delta seems to be the same in all the dimensions of w, variance of I\delta. Should not  the variance be scaled proportionally by the  magnitude of each parameter. Otherwise the final Deviation measure can be highly influenced and bias by some parameters based on their magnitude.  Can you please explain?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents an interesting framework for uncertainty-based active learning. I  think the ideas presented are interested but there is a couple of topics that need further attention / explanation. It would be interesting to have more insight on how the size of the parameter space affects the computational complexity and the performance of the proposed algorithm and there is little of that in the paper in its current form.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Dsk8
content.comment:
$\bullet$ When to sampling w for large models -- 

: The experimental results for various values of $N$ (=number of samples of each parameter leading to $N$ hypothesis in selecting the unlabeled samples) are included in Appendix I. It is observed that there are no significant performance differences when $N \ge 5$. The number of query samples for a smaller network (for classifying MNIST) is much smaller than that for a larger model (for classifying CIFAR 100), and this would mean we would need to be fairly accurate in selecting the smaller number of query samples for smaller network requiring $N$ to be large and less accurate when selecting a larger number of query sample which does not require $N$ to be large.
When $N$ is small, the sample order by disagree ratio $D$  may not be consistent with that obtained from empirical LPDR, but the top $q$ samples (top $q$ samples from disagree ratio and top $q$ samples from empirical LPDR) are consistent as the $\sigma$ is set such that it satisfies $\rho_{_S} (h_n, \hat{h}) = q/m$ where $m$ is the number of unlabeled samples. The samples selected by empirical LPDR and $D$ match 95-98\% in Figure 7b in Appendix C. We set $N=100$ (to compare with MC_BALD's 100 dropouts), and the description of hyperparameters in the experiments is moved from Appendix to the main body. In addition, the use of $D$ (instead of empirical LPDR to reduce sampling time) in our algorithm performs well in comparison with other SOTA active learning algorithms for the deep networks.	


$\bullet$ Is the whole parameter set -- 

: The parameters in the last layer are sampled in the experiments for computation efficiency as there is no significant performance difference between DRAL$^+$ with sampling every parameter and DRAL$^+$ with sampling last layer's parameters, and the results of the performance comparison between two methods on MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 are added in Appendix. We did not consider sampling only a few parameters of the last layer. If only a few of the last layer is sampled, it may not perform well since it will miss the disagreement in the non-sampling dimension, and in terms of computational efficiency, sampling only a few parameters in the last layer has almost the same computational complexity as sampling all parameters in the last layer since inner dot product followed by exponentiation and normalization is evaluated collectively. 



$\bullet$ A concern is that the results are fine --
: As a result of a one-to-one comparison of 7 algorithms for DRAL$^+$ on 6 datasets, DRAL$^+$ consistently outperforms others on all datasets. Furthermore, DRAL$^+$ shows significant performance improvement in most cases (39 out of 42). The details are added in Table 2. The numbers of sampled and whole parameters for each experimental setting are added to Table 1.
As mentioned, when sampling $\boldsymbol{w}$, $\sigma$ is the same in all dimensions regardless of the magnitude of each parameter and is updated at the following sampling. We have observed a drop in performance when we set $\sigma$ or variance of each component to be proportional to the magnitude of the parameter- when we set $\sigma$ to be proportional to the magnitude of a parameter, the perturbation is dominated in the direction of the stronger parameter dimension and we do not have a uniform perturbation around the parameter setting.


$\bullet$ Reply to summary --

: The running time of the proposed algorithm is comparable with entropy-based uncertainty sampling even if the parameter space is very large. The results of running time for all experiments are added to Appendix J. The performance of the proposed algorithm is compared with other high-performing algorithms on 6 datasets with 3 networks, and the proposed algorithm outperforms all other algorithms.

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive comments and suggestions, especially to all reviewers' comments that the idea of this paper is interesting and the experimental results are promising.

The comments motivated us to revise the manuscript in a more kind, insightful, and rigorous manner. The detailed responses to comments are in replies to comments, and we list out the emphasizing as follows: 

$\bullet$ Description of Conjectures was revised by following the comments. We polished the conjectures, clarification the proofs, and additionally provide the theoretical verification in linear classifiers using duality and geometry. The conjectures are more grounded theoretically or intuitively.
    
$\bullet$ We highlighted the motivation for introducing the disagree ratio (DR) and that the DR is a measure naturally derived from the definition of LPDR. We emphasize that the DR is the consequent algorithm from the LPDR. Therefore, in the manuscript, we summarize the study about LPDR, empirical LPDR, and rank of (empirical) LPDR in the same section, and the induced practical algorithm with DR is stated in algorithm section.

$\bullet$ As a result of one-to-one comparison of 7 algorithms for DRAL$^+$ on 6 datasets, DRAL$^+$ consistently outperforms others on all datasets. Furthermore, DRAL$^+$ shows significant performance improvement in most cases (39 out of 42--the p-value is less than 0.05 in one-sample t-test for the performance differences).
    
$\bullet$ The details of the experimental settings were moved from the appendix to the main body and additional experiments were conducted on the robustness of the proposed algorithm for the sampling layer of the model and the initial labeled size.
    
We did our best to address the reviewers' various comments. Please see the detailed responses and revised manuscript in which red colored characters are used to point out the revised part.
